tldr: To make the most of human motion data, the authors developed an open-source, 88 cm-tall humanoid named "Bridge" capable of backflips and single-leg balancing, built through a co-design framework that jointly optimizes robot morphology and reinforcement learning controllers.
hero_caption: The proposed co-design pipeline and the hardware demonstrations of the developed humanoid "Bridge." By iterating through actuator selection, link geometry optimization, and control policy training and validation, the real robot successfully performs highly dynamic whole-body coordination tasks like backflips.
overview:
When teaching humanoid robots to move with human-like fluidity, human motion capture data is the most valuable source of information. In conventional robot development, however, hardware and software are strictly decoupled: mechanical engineers design the physical robot based on intuition, experience, and mechanical convenience, and control engineers later attempt to control this fixed body using reinforcement learning. Under this paradigm, software is forced to compensate for hardware bottlenecks like poor joint placement, limited ranges of motion, and motor output limits. This unavoidably leads to unnatural, awkward motions and physically infeasible poses.

To tackle this, the authors built a "co-design" framework that jointly optimizes robot morphology and whole-body control in a closed loop. Starting from the human SMPL body model with tentative, small actuators placed at the joints, reinforcement learning policies are trained in a simulation environment incorporating experimentally measured torque-speed curves. The pipeline then pinpoints specific joints that failed due to insufficient torque or velocity, upgrades them with larger motors, and geometrically re-optimizes link lengths and mass distributions in a failure-guided iterative cycle.

In addition, they introduce a "Human-likeness Metric" that combines geometric retargeting fidelity to human movement with dynamic tracking performance under closed-loop control. They evaluated the approach against existing open-source small humanoids (Bumi, K1, and Toddlerbot). The resulting robot "Bridge"—standing 88 cm tall and weighing 13 kg—outperformed all existing platforms across every metric, achieving a 94.83% motion success rate. The hardware design files and trained control policies are released as fully open source.
contributions: Formulated a novel "Human-likeness Metric" that jointly evaluates kinematic retargeting fidelity to human movement and dynamic tracking performance under closed-loop control.
Proposed an iterative morphology-control co-design framework that incorporates physical actuator envelopes and measured performance limits, using tracking failures to identify bottleneck joints.
Realized the optimal morphology into "Bridge," an open-source 88 cm-tall, 21-DoF humanoid platform released alongside its whole-body control policies.

Demonstrated through large-scale human motion datasets that Bridge significantly outperforms comparable platforms in tracking fidelity and success rate, validated with challenging maneuvers on hardware like backflips and single-leg balance.

sections.heading: Why Shouldn't We Build Hardware and Control Separately?
sections.summary: This section points out that the conventional decoupled paradigm—isolating hardware design from control learning—is a critical bottleneck in building general-purpose humanoids that leverage human motion data. To solve this, the authors propose a co-design framework optimizing kinematic and dynamic fidelity simultaneously, validated on the physical robot "Bridge."
sections.details:
To deploy humanoid robots as general-purpose agents in human-centric environments, transferring abundant human behavioral data directly into robot skills is ideal. Today, however, hardware development and whole-body control research operate largely in isolation.

Conventional hardware design prioritizes actuator placement, ease of manufacturing, and rule-of-thumb proportions, with little regard for the specific workspaces or torque profiles required by downstream reinforcement learning controllers. Control researchers, in turn, must accept this fixed morphology and use reinforcement learning to compensate for unnatural kinematics and insufficient motor torque. As a result, no matter how long the policies train in simulation, the motions often end up awkward or fail due to torque saturation.

This paper starts from that disconnect. The authors developed an iterative co-design framework that accurately mirrors the kinematics of the human SMPL model while accounting for physical actuator dimensions, torque limits, and velocity constraints, using closed-loop control performance in simulation as feedback for hardware updates.

Furthermore, to quantify "human-likeness," they introduced a new metric combining kinematic retargeting error (geometric discrepancy) with closed-loop dynamic tracking error (physical discrepancy). The morphology derived through this framework became "Bridge," an 88 cm-tall, 21-DoF humanoid platform. Both the hardware files and control policies are fully open-sourced to serve as a foundation for Physical AI research.

sections.heading: Taking Co-Design from Pure Simulation into the Physical World
sections.summary: The authors review prior literature on robot co-design and deep reinforcement learning for whole-body control. While previous co-design works stayed within simulation and neglected real-world actuator constraints, this work stands out by completing the loop all the way to physical hardware fabrication.
sections.details:
The concept of robot co-design—jointly optimizing robot morphology and control—has a long history spanning genetic algorithms, deep generative models, and diffusion frameworks. Most prior studies, however, were limited to grid worlds or simplified toy models in simulation. They neglected unglamorous physical realities like off-the-shelf actuator envelopes, wiring space, bearing placements, and empirical torque-speed curves. Consequently, morphologies produced in simulation could rarely be built in the real world.

Meanwhile, in humanoid whole-body control, recent advances in simulators and reinforcement learning (RL) have driven impressive progress in motion tracking, rough-terrain locomotion, and Sim-to-Real transfer. Yet, these methods uniformly assume a fixed morphology, never leveraging controller performance as a signal to improve the physical hardware.

Although ML-oriented, open-source small humanoids like "ToddlerBot" have appeared recently, their morphologies were still hand-tuned by human engineers. This work presents the first systematic humanoid co-design framework that feeds dynamic tracking performance directly into hardware design while fully guaranteeing real-world manufacturability.

sections.heading: Learning from Failure: 4 Steps to Optimize Actuators and Skeletal Linkages
sections.summary: This section explains the proposed co-design algorithm across four stages: waist DoF compression, actuator-aware URDF generation, dynamic evaluation via control policies, and iterative failure-guided actuator refinement for saturated joints.
sections.details:
The core insight of this method is treating humanoid morphology and whole-body locomotion control not as sequential steps, but as coupled design variables solved simultaneously. The process unfolds across four stages:

### 3.1 DoF Compression
The design starts from a 23-DoF model capturing primary human SMPL joints. To leave interior space for batteries within an 88 cm frame, the 3-DoF waist (roll, pitch, yaw) had to be reduced to 1 DoF. Instead of picking an axis arbitrarily, the selection was made in two steps. First, human motions were kinematically retargeted onto three two-axis combinations; "roll + yaw" yielded the lowest kinematic retargeting error $e_{\mathrm{kin}}$. Next, two 21-DoF candidate models (roll-only vs. yaw-only) were trained with control policies to compare their closed-loop dynamic tracking error $e_{\mathrm{dyn}}$. The yaw-only waist configuration achieved superior tracking and was selected.

### 3.2 Actuator-aware Robot Instantiation
Ideal kinematic models often assume that multi-axis joints, such as the shoulder or hip, have intersecting axes at a single point. Real motors have physical volume, making zero-offset intersection impossible. The authors placed the primary flexion/extension pitch axis at the anatomical joint center and shifted the roll and yaw axes along the limb axis. Factoring in inter-motor clearance $\delta_{i,i+1}$, link lengths and mass properties were computed, and structural parameters $\theta$ were optimized to minimize motion retargeting error, generating a URDF. Initially, the smallest, lightest actuator model was assigned to every joint.

### 3.3 Motion-based Robot Evaluation
Using the generated candidate URDF, a base trained policy was fine-tuned for each reference motion trajectory $\tau$ to assess dynamic tracking. Here, realistic torque-speed limits calibrated from physical experiments were strictly enforced. The proportion of motions completed without falling and within a tracking error threshold was recorded as the motion coverage rate $R_{\mathrm{motion}}$.

### 3.4 Failure-Guided Robot Refinement
For failed motions, peak actuator utilization $\rho_j$ across joints was analyzed. A joint was identified as a true physical bottleneck only if its torque or velocity repeatedly saturated across different random seeds, and artificially lifting its limits allowed the motion to succeed. The actuator at that joint was then upgraded to a more powerful (and heavier/bulkier) model. Because new motors change overall mass distribution and link dimensions, the pipeline loops back to Step 3.2 to regenerate the URDF and re-test all motions. Repeating this cycle until the coverage target is met yields an optimal 21-DoF morphology with sufficient power and minimal extra weight.

sections.heading: Dominating Baselines in Motion Tracking and Agile Real-World Execution
sections.summary: Using the proposed Human-likeness Metric, Bridge was evaluated against existing small humanoids (Bumi, K1, Toddlerbot). Bridge achieved skeletal proportions closest to humans, the highest tracking success rate, and faster training convergence, while successfully demonstrating backflips and single-leg balance on hardware.
sections.details:
The experiments evaluated the co-design framework across objective metrics, subjective assessments, and physical robot deployments.

### 4.1 Human-likeness Metric
To assess robot morphology and controller pairs, the authors defined a Human-likeness score $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{HL}}$ weighting kinematic error $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{kin}}$ (geometric fidelity to human anatomy) and dynamic tracking error $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{dyn}}$ (tracking fidelity under physical simulation) equally at 0.5. The final Bridge design incorporated 10 Nm-class actuators for all upper-body joints, 55 Nm-class actuators for hip and knee pitch axes, and 25 Nm-class actuators for other joints, including parallel-link ankles.

### 4.2 Objective Evaluation: Skeletal Proportions and Tracking Accuracy
Comparing objective metrics against existing platforms (Bumi, K1, ToddlerBot), Bridge achieved the highest Human-likeness score ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{HL}} = 0.5252$). While average segment length scale ratios relative to the SMPL model were distorted on ToddlerBot (1.17), K1 (1.34), and Bumi (1.38), Bridge maintained a near-human ratio of 1.02.

In tracking benchmarks across large motion datasets (LaFAN1 and bones_seed) using the state-of-the-art whole-body controller "SONIC," Bridge reached an overall success rate of 94.83%. The difference was especially striking in the "Highly Dynamic" category, where Bridge achieved a 94.50% success rate, outperforming the runner-up K1 (89.80%) by 4.70 percentage points. In imitation learning with "BeyondMimic" on dance tasks, Bridge also converged faster and reached lower value function losses.

### 4.3 Subjective and Qualitative Real-World Validation
In balance and visual naturalness, Bridge naturally kept its center of mass over the support foot during toe-stands and single-leg balance without awkward joint contortions. Hardware experiments further confirmed agile physical capability, cleanly performing single-leg balance, Charleston dance steps, full-body VR teleoperation, and dynamic backflips.

Starting from an ideal slender model on the far left, incorporating actuator limits and upgrading bottleneck motors dramatically boosts the motion success rate (SR) from 44.63% to 94.83% (second from right, selected model) while maintaining low kinematic error ($\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{kin}}$).

Bridge (blue line) exhibits minimal deviation across all body segments, closely preserving natural human proportions compared to other platforms.

Bridge (solid blue line) converges markedly faster from early training and reaches the lowest final loss, confirming its physical structure is inherently easier for control policies to drive.

Compared to the human reference (SMPL, far left), Bridge (far right) correctly positions its center of mass (red circle) over the support foot (green circle), maintaining stable, natural balance even in bent-over and tiptoe postures.

sections.heading: Summary and Next Steps: Miniature Limits and Next-Gen Actuation
sections.summary: The paper concludes by highlighting Bridge as an open-source platform achieving human-like motion via morphology-control co-design, pointing to tendon-driven mechanisms and scaling to life-size as avenues for future work.
sections.details:
This work proposed a humanoid morphology-control co-design pipeline designed to transfer human behavioral data seamlessly, culminating in the open-source 88 cm humanoid "Bridge." By using closed-loop control failures as direct signals to update hardware rather than designing mechanics in isolation, the system achieved exceptional dynamic tracking fidelity.

However, the authors openly acknowledge two main limitations in the current design.

First, all joints rely on conventional rotary actuators (brushless motors with gear reducers). Placing motors directly at joint locations bulks up the limbs and increases limb inertia. Adopting tendon-driven mechanisms could relocate heavy actuators to the torso, unlocking more slender limbs and lighter dynamic behavior closer to human anatomy.

Second, while the 88 cm height makes the platform accessible and affordable for research labs, it inherently limits manipulation payload and reaching workspace. To interact with real-world tools and human-scale infrastructure, scaling this co-design framework up to a life-sized humanoid remains an essential next step.

takeaways: Rather than tuning control on fixed hardware, failure-guided co-design—using controller failures (torque and velocity saturation) as signals to refine hardware—is highly effective for pushing physical limits.
Closing the gap between kinematic models and real actuators requires modeling multi-axis offsets and empirical torque-speed limits in simulation right from the start.

Human-likeness in humanoids should be judged not by skeletal geometry alone, but through an integrated metric ($\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{HL}}$) that accounts for dynamic tracking under closed-loop physical simulation.
limitations: Relying entirely on direct rotary actuators at joint locations structurally limits how much joint volume and limb inertia can be reduced.
Standing 88 cm tall and weighing 13 kg, the robot lacks the payload and physical reach required for functional real-world manipulation with human-sized tools and furniture.
